newsitem.title: USA: Boycott to hit Texaco image more than bottom line.
newsitem.headline: Boycott to hit Texaco image more than bottom line.

text.p: If previous boycott battles against oil companies are anything to go by then the efforts by Jesse Jackson's coalition against Texaco Inc are unlikely to have much financial impact on the company, analysts and advocates said.
But some say the embarrassment of a sustained media focus on the company's race record may be enough to force action by the company.
On Tuesday, Jesse Jackson and a coalition of civil rights leaders urged U.S. consumers to boycott Texaco products until a discrimination suit pending since 1994 is settled.
The suit relit headlines this week after transcripts of a meeting -- later proved partially incorrect -- reported top Texaco leaders using racial epithets to describe minority employees.

"Like past boycotts of other oil companies, we believe that (Jesse) Jackson's call to boycott Texaco stations will have little impact on the financial performance of Texaco," said oil analyst Steve Pfeifer of PaineWebber.
PaineWebber estimates that even an effective boycott against Texaco could only reduce annual U.S. marketing earnings by 10 to 20 percent, or $11 to $22 million.
That sacrifice would pale compared to expected 1996 company earnings of $1.5 billion from worldwide oil and gas operations.
"In general most consumers focus on price, convenience and location, not politics," said Pfeifer.
Economic boycotts against oil giants in recent years have rarely hit oil companies very hard in the pocketbook, observers say, although they have prodded some changes in corporate policy.
In mid-1995 a consumer boycott in Europe called by Greenpeace against Royal Dutch/Shell stations had little financial impact, despite the firebombing of some Shell stations in Germany.
Greenpeace was protesting against the company's plans to dump the giant Brent Spar platform in deep waters in the north Atlantic, charging the plan was not environmentally sound.

Despite egg on its face from the Brent Spar and even more damaging subsequent publicity about its role in Nigeria, Royal Dutch/Shell Group shares have advanced 35 percent since mid-1995, Pfeifer points out.
Bob Bassman, a U.S. lawyer who represents gasoline marketers, says brand loyalty and convenience have helped inoculate oil companies from serious boycott damage.
"In the service station business the right corner is everything," keeping customers coming despite the winds of political controversy, he adds.
But consumer advocate Ralph Nader said the Texaco boycott could indeed succeed given the keen competition that exists among gasoline retailers in some parts of the country.
"People can very easily go to another station across the street," said Nader.
Most analysts, however, say it is difficult in today's global market to bring large companies to their knees.

"When you talk of a firm that is on a national or international scope it is very hard to get people together to deny business," said Paul Uselding, a professor of American Economic and Business History at the Univeristy of Illinois in Chicago.
"It's very difficult to keep up the pressure on large well-capitalized firms. The boycott in the traditional sense as economic punishment is not very effective," Uselding said.
Uselding adds that it is more the public scrutiny and media attention that most large companies fear.
"Many boycotts that are economic in nature are intended to mobilize intense media scrutiny on the issue and most managers don't like the attention," said the professor.
Most companies that are the focus of such boycotts usually capitulate or make only enough concessions to turn off the spotlight, said Uselding.

Intense public pressure on Exxon Corp following its spillage of 35,000 tonnes of crude oil in 1989 along the Alaskan Coast, for example, forced reluctant executives to pay $2.5 billion alone in cleanup and upgrade its long-term environmental policies.

The scrutiny on "Exxon worked to some extent in holding their feet to the fire on what was a broad public concern," said Edwin Rothschild, head of the Washington D.C.-based consumer advocacy group, Citizen Action.
As for the boycott against Texaco, Rothschild said he doubts the company would be hurt financially "but will have the visible consequence of putting Texaco and the oil industry on the spot."
